lesson.title: The Unwritten Rules That Run Our Lives: Social Norms
lesson.summary: Social norms are the shared, often unspoken, expectations within a group or culture about which behaviors, attitudes, and values are appropriate, and they guide an enormous amount of everyday behavior without most people ever consciously thinking about them.
lesson.body:
Much of psychology's power comes from studying things that feel obvious or invisible in ordinary life and subjecting them to careful, controlled observation, which is part of what makes psychology a science rather than simply organized common sense. Social norms are a good example of exactly this kind of hidden structure. We rarely notice the norm that governs how much personal space to leave between ourselves and a stranger in an elevator, or how loudly to speak in a library, until someone violates it, at which point the discomfort we feel reveals just how strongly the norm was operating all along.

Psychologists commonly distinguish between two broad kinds of social norms. Descriptive norms describe what people actually tend to do in a given situation, essentially what is common or typical. Injunctive norms describe what people believe ought to be done, what is approved of or disapproved of by the group, regardless of how many people actually comply. These two types of norms usually point in the same direction, but not always, and research associated with Robert Cialdini and colleagues has shown that they can even work against each other, for instance when a sign describing littering as a common problem, a descriptive norm, inadvertently signals that littering is normal and thereby increases it, compared to a message emphasizing that littering is disapproved of, an injunctive norm.

A classic demonstration of how social norms actually form comes from Muzafer Sherif's research in the 1930s using the autokinetic effect, a visual illusion in which a small, stationary point of light in an otherwise completely dark room appears to drift or move, because the brain has no fixed reference point to judge it against. When individuals estimated how far the light moved while alone, their guesses varied widely from person to person. But when Sherif placed people in small groups and had them call out their estimates aloud, the individual estimates gradually converged on a shared figure, a group norm, even though the light was not actually moving at all. Strikingly, when those same individuals were later tested alone again, many continued to give answers close to the group's norm rather than reverting to their original independent estimate, suggesting the norm had genuinely become internalized rather than just publicly performed.

Social norms vary enormously across cultures, subcultures, and even specific situations within the same culture, but the underlying psychological function is similar everywhere: norms reduce uncertainty about how to behave, especially in ambiguous situations, and they coordinate behavior across large groups of people who may never interact directly. Understanding how norms form and operate is the foundation for the next concept, a broader account of how other people influence our thoughts, feelings, and behavior known as social influence theory.
